newsitem.title: USA: Stocks fall, dollar hits high against yen.
newsitem.headline: Stocks fall, dollar hits high against yen.

text.p: Stocks gave up early gains and ended lower Monday as investors awaited fresh economic data, while the dollar climbed to its highest level against the Japanese yen in 3-1/2 years on uncertainty about Japan's new government.
Bonds lost ground. Gold and oil ended little changed.

The Dow Jones industrial average fell 34.29 points to close at 5,972.73, after being up more than 35 points early in the day. In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,530 to 865 on moderate volume of 383 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Investors braced for an onslaught of economic numbers, including figures on wages due on Tuesday, the economy's third-quarter performance, due on Wednesday, and the October employment report, due on Friday.

"Some investors are locking in profits ahead of several important economic indicators due to be released later this week," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.

Analysts said the market's retreat stemmed from Wall Street concerns that the Democrats will retake the House of Representatives in the election and to tax-loss related selling by mutual funds in the final week of the month.

"There's nothing fundamentally wrong with the market. But there's the same worry that the Democrats will take Congress in addition to the presidency and that causes consternation among fund managers," said Thom Brown, a managing director at Rutherford Brown & Catherwood.
He said individual investors would likely complete their tax-loss selling in November. "It's going to mitigate against seeing the market go a lot higher."
Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. said, "The market is shifting its attention to the economy and interest rates, a combination that will dominate this week."
With the bulk of third-quarter corporate earnings out, most of the good news is out of the market.

In currency markets, the dollar rose again vs. the yen as Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto continued to struggle to stitch together a government more than a week after Japan's Oct. 20 election.

Most politicians and analysts now expect Hashimoto to head into a new session of parliament at the head of a minority government, making another election a constant threat and forcing investors who crave political stability to pull their money out of yen-based assets and put it to work elsewhere.
"People are attributing it to a lack of a political settlement in Japan," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan, in New York.
The dollar rose to 114.38 yen on Monday -- its highest since April 1993, when it reached 115.20 -- before settling at 114.21 yen in U.S. trading, up from 113.42 late Friday.
Low Japanese interest rates also fuelled the move out of yen-based assets into investments based in dollars and other major currencies, traders said.
The dollar's rise against the yen did not translate into gains against other major currencies.
The dollar fell to 1.5190 German marks late in New York from 1.5200 late on Friday, and to 1.2611 Swiss francs from 1.2617. The pound rose to $1.6128 from $1.6048 on Friday.
In the bond market, the 30-year Treasury bond fell about a quarter point, raising its yield to 6.84 percent from 6.82 percent on Friday.
Elsewhere, crude oil for December delivery fell 1 cent to $24.85 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange. December gold ended unchanged at $384.60 an ounce.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 rose 2.9 points to 4,025.3 while Tokyo's 225-issue Nikkei average added 145.44 points to 20,885.41.
